name: Idiopathic short stature

lead: Idiopathic short stature (ISS) is the label paediatric endocrinologists use for a child who is well below average height for their age and sex, where a full evaluation finds no hormonal, nutritional, genetic-syndrome or other disease explaining it. It matters for height because, in the United States and several other countries, ISS is a regulator-approved indication for growth hormone therapy intended to raise adult height.

The diagnosis is a medical route rather than a lifestyle one: it is applied to children whose growth plates are still open, and the clinical literature describes both treatment results (typically modest average gains in adult height) and ongoing debate about who should be treated. Researchers are also finding genetic variants behind some cases once labelled idiopathic.

paras: A child is referred for slow growth or short height, and a specialist rules out other causes through history, examination, bone-age imaging and blood tests, sometimes including genetic testing. If ISS is diagnosed, options discussed in the guidelines include monitoring or a course of daily injected growth hormone prescribed and supervised by a paediatric endocrinologist. Some trials have also tested aromatase inhibitors in boys during puberty. Treatment runs for years and is followed with regular growth measurements.

Growth hormone therapy involves daily injections, regular clinic follow-up and cost, and reviews describe the extra adult height as variable and often modest. Aromatase inhibitors are used off-label in this setting and one trial arm studied cognitive effects in boys. Guidelines describe ISS as a controversial treatment indication and recommend individual weighing of benefits and risks. Growth hormone is prescription-only and is not appropriate for adults with closed growth plates.

angle.text: The diagnosis opens a medical route to height treatment in childhood: if a specialist confirms ISS, growth hormone may be prescribed to raise adult height. The size of the gain varies between studies, and it applies only while growth plates are open.

lead: Idiopathic short stature (ISS) is a clinical term for a child whose height is well below the average for age and sex when evaluation finds no specific cause. A 2008 international consensus statement defined it by a height more than 2 standard deviations below the mean, without findings of disease on a complete evaluation by a paediatric endocrinologist, including stimulated growth hormone testing [1]. The word 'idiopathic' means the cause is not known; a 2024 review describes ISS as not a single diagnosis but a heterogeneous group of short, often slowly growing children [2].

For people interested in height, ISS is relevant because it is one of the pathways through which growth hormone (GH) is prescribed to increase adult height. Regulators in the United States and several other countries approved GH for ISS, and the US lists it among eight FDA-approved paediatric GH indications [3]. Clinical trials have measured how much taller treated children become compared with untreated children, and others have examined aromatase inhibitors, which slow bone maturation by lowering estrogen, in boys during puberty [4].

The topic has long been discussed in the medical literature as a point of debate. Guidelines from the Pediatric Endocrine Society note that ISS remains a controversial indication and that it can be hard to separate from GH deficiency and primary IGF-I deficiency [5]. Advances in genetic testing are also reducing the pool of children labelled idiopathic by identifying specific gene variants [2][6].
infobox: Height below -2 SD with no identified cause [1]

paras: The 2008 consensus statement from the Growth Hormone Research Society, the Lawson Wilkins Pediatric Endocrine Society and the European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology defines ISS auxologically, meaning by measurement: height below -2 SD score and no evidence of disease after a complete evaluation, including stimulated GH levels [1]. It adds that ISS may be a risk factor for psychosocial problems, but true psychopathology is rare [1]. Wikipedia notes that the term has been in use since at least 1975, and that a 2003 request by Eli Lilly to the FDA proposed a cutoff of about 2.25 SD below the mean (roughly the shortest 1.2 percent of the population) [7].

A 2024 Endocrine Practice review says many genetic, nutritional, psychological, illness-related and hormonal causes must be excluded before a child is labelled idiopathic, and that most remaining cases are thought to be polygenic [2]. Physical examination for subtle skeletal disproportion is advised because newly recognised genes often act in growth plate biology [2].

Because ISS is a diagnosis of exclusion, it groups together children with different biological explanations. A 2025 review reports newly identified pathogenic variants in genes including FBN1, IHH, NPR2, ACAN, FGFR3, COMP and others, with sequencing studies finding a diagnostic yield up to 33 percent in children previously labelled ISS [6]. Genotype-specific treatments are emerging [6]. A registered cohort study of ISS patients with genome-wide analysis is also under way [8].

Recombinant human GH, available since the mid-1980s, was first used for children with severe GH deficiency and later studied in other conditions, including ISS [9]. A 2022 review lists ISS among FDA-approved paediatric indications [3]. Treatment is a prescription injection overseen by specialists, and guidelines recommend individualised decisions weighing benefits and risks [5].

Older clinical reviews reported that spontaneous adult height in ISS was often close to the children's target height, and that GH led to adult height not significantly above the pre-treatment prediction in most reports [10]. More recent trials examine GH as an add-on, for example a multicentre Chinese phase 3 trial randomising 481 prepubertal children to daily somatropin or no treatment for 52 weeks [11].

Because estrogen drives growth plate closure in puberty, aromatase inhibitors have been compared with GH, and with the two combined, in a randomised three-arm trial of 76 pubertal boys with severe ISS [4]. A separate randomised trial examined cognitive effects of aromatase inhibitor therapy in peripubertal boys [12]. Newer agents such as vosoritide are being tested in registered phase 2 studies [13].

The consensus statement notes that short stature can be a psychosocial risk factor in some children [1]. A randomised placebo-controlled trial specifically examined whether GH therapy changes short-stature-related distress [14][15]. Wikipedia records that a 2006 critical review found some evidence that hormone treatment might not significantly improve psychosocial functioning, and that commentators have debated treatment cost and whether treating ISS shifts the stigma to the next shortest group [7].

Human studies include the randomised GH trials in prepubertal and pubertal children [11][4], observational work on spontaneous adult height [10], the placebo-controlled distress trial [14], and consensus and guideline documents [1][5]. Outcomes are reported as average differences in height or height SDS between groups, and results vary by dose, age and duration. Ongoing registered studies include phase 2 and phase 3 trials of other agents [13] and a genomics cohort [8].

timeline.event: The term idiopathic short stature appears in medical use (per Wikipedia) [7].
Recombinant human GH replaces pituitary-derived GH, enabling wider study of its use [9].
Eli Lilly submits trial data to the FDA seeking an ISS indication for GH [7].
International consensus statement on ISS diagnosis and treatment is published [1].
Pediatric Endocrine Society publishes updated GH and IGF-I guidelines covering ISS [5].
Reviews describe a growing role for genetic testing in ISS evaluation [2].
